questions.q: Why do we need to separate substances?
questions.a: To remove harmful or useless parts, and to get useful components separately (grain from stalk).

questions.q: Name one separation you see in the kitchen.
questions.a: Filtering tea leaves, or draining water from boiled rice.

questions.q: What happens if we do not remove impurities from food?
questions.a: Pebbles and dust can break teeth and harm health.

questions.q: When is handpicking used for separation?
questions.a: When unwanted bits are few and large enough to pick - stones from dal.

questions.q: How does winnowing separate grain from husk?
questions.a: Wind blows the light husk away while the heavy grain falls straight down.
Beating stalks to free the grain, done by bullocks or machines (threshers).

questions.q: How does sieving separate a mixture?
questions.a: Fine particles pass through the sieve holes; bigger bits stay behind.
Heavy particles settle in water (sedimentation); the clear top water is poured off (decantation).

questions.q: Name one use of sedimentation at home.
questions.a: Letting muddy water settle before pouring the clearer water out.

questions.q: How is salt recovered from salt solution?
questions.a: By evaporating the water - salt crystals remain in the dish.

questions.q: Why does the salt stay behind when water evaporates?
questions.a: Salt does not evaporate; only the water leaves as vapour.

questions.q: Can this method give back the water too? How?
questions.a: Yes - by condensing the vapour on a cold surface (distillation).
